about: Enemy commanders' temperament traits (DESIGN §4b). Generated by tools/build-traits.mjs from tools/data/cs-traits-verified.json; never edit by hand. Traits are history (each claim with its opened sources); their effects are game rules (src/franchise/tuning.js TRAITS).
method: Each URL below was opened via WebFetch and, where the host permitted, re-checked verbatim with curl. npshistory.com blocks curl (403), so its quotes are as returned by WebFetch's page reader. Quotes are page text, not paginated; 'page' is a section or caption. Wikipedia, search snippets and unopened books (Symonds, McDonough, Cozzens, McWhiney, Hallock, Daniel, Roland, Williams, Parks, Warner, Hughes & Stonesifer, Official Records volumes) were NOT counted. Official Records on ehistory.osu.edu returned 403; the only OR text opened is Hardee's Perryville report at perryvillebattlefield.org.
independence: ABT pages are counted as one organisation: where a trait rests on several ABT pages plus nothing else, it is not called Verified.
notRun: No OR volume, HathiTrust, archive.org book or Google Books preview was opened; Official Records citations from the earlier pass remain unverified.

aggressive.label: Quick to attack
aggressive.effect: Game rule: his formations begin their attacks and reserve moves 20 s sooner, a reserve commits when an enemy comes within 1.3 times the usual distance, and a stopped or repulsed attacker goes forward again in half the time.

impetuous.label: Goes in without waiting
impetuous.brief: steps off early and waits less for the formations beside it
impetuous.effect: Game rule: his formations step off 10 s before their set time and wait only a quarter as long for the formations beside them.

cautious.label: Holds back
cautious.brief: starts later, keeps reserves back longer and falls back sooner
cautious.effect: Game rule: his formations begin attacks and reserve moves 20 s later, a reserve commits only when an enemy is within 0.7 times the usual distance, a stopped march is renewed 1.5 times more slowly, and a shaken formation falls back when the nearest enemy outnumbers it.

stubborn.label: Holds on
stubborn.brief: gives ground only against heavier odds
stubborn.effect: Game rule: a formation holding its ground falls back only when the nearest enemy has 1.6 times its men (usually: any more men).

methodical.label: Prepares and coordinates
methodical.brief: waits to move with the formations beside it
methodical.effect: Game rule: once begun, an attacker or reserve waits up to 45 s for the other formations sharing its objective, and never renews a stopped march sooner than usual.

skilled-defender.label: Defends well
skilled-defender.brief: counter-attacks a breakthrough and takes nearby cover
skilled-defender.effect: Game rule: a holding brigade counter-attacks an enemy that breaks into its position or past a routing friend within 350 m, and before the enemy comes within 250 m it moves once to better cover within 100 m.

slow.label: Slow to act
slow.brief: reacts and renews its orders more slowly
slow.effect: Game rule: his formations decide only every 2nd time the AI looks (every 1 s instead of 0.5 s at Veteran) and renew a stopped march 1.5 times more slowly.

reckless.label: Led from the front
reckless.brief: he is more likely to be hit
reckless.effect: Game rule: he rides where the fighting is, so fire within 180 m of him (usually 120 m) puts him at risk of being wounded or killed.

Albert Sidney Johnston.provenanceNote: 'aggressive' is Verified (3 opened sources, 2 independent organisations). 'reckless' is a judgment: both ABT pages (same organisation, so not independent) say he rode ahead of his troops; NPS frames the same moment as directing reserves. Behaviour agreed, label contested. Suggest the game text say 'led from the front' rather than 'reckless'.

evidence.claim: Johnston planned and launched the 6 April 1862 attack on Grant at Pittsburg Landing, intending to strike a day earlier before rain delayed him, to beat Buell's arrival.

evidence.claim: Johnston was hit behind the right knee and bled to death on 6 April 1862 while forward of his main line. ABT says he rode ahead of / too far ahead of his troops; NPS says he was personally directing reserves.
evidence.researchNote: The 'tourniquet in pocket' detail is in both ABT and NPS; the 'sent his surgeon away' detail was NOT found in any opened source and is dropped.

Leonidas Polk.provenanceNote: Behaviour (delay, not attacking when ordered) is agreed by all sources; cause and blame are Bragg's accusation vs NPS's miscommunication account. Game text should describe the delay, not assert disobedience. Note ABT also credits Polk's corps with taking the Round Forest twice (TN Encyclopedia) and 'dogged fighting' (NCpedia).

evidence.claim: At Chickamauga on 20 Sept 1863 the planned dawn attack on the Confederate right did not go in until about 9:30 A.M. Bragg accused Polk (commanding the right wing) of 'critically delaying orders'; NPS attributes the delay to miscommunication, so the delay is agreed and the blame is disputed.

Patrick R. Cleburne.provenanceNote: Arkansas entry gives '4,000 men held back 15,000' at Ringgold; Tennessee Encyclopedia gives 5,500 vs 15,000 at Tunnel Hill. Numbers differ by source; do not hard-code them. Stones River exhaustion note: NPS series quotes Cleburne that exhaustion, not Union fire, ended the advance.

evidence.claim: His men spearheaded Hardee's 31 Dec 1862 attack on the Union right at Stones River (Bragg praised the division); he stayed in command at Perryville despite two wounds; he was killed leading the assault on the Franklin breastworks on 30 Nov 1864.

James R. Chalmers.provenanceNote: The NPS people page dates Munfordville to November 1862; every other source says 14-17 Sept 1862 (NPS page is wrong on the date). MUST-INCLUDE note for the game: NPS says Chalmers 'commanded the Confederate force on the field in the attack on Fort Pillow, Tennessee, which ended with a massacre of surrender[ed] Federal African American soldiers' (nps.gov/people/james-ronald-chalmers.htm); the NPS Civil War Sites battle page says 'Many accused the Confederates of perpetrating a massacre ... and that controversy continues today'. The Shiloh part of the earlier aggressive claim is not supported by an opened source with detail and is dropped.

Benjamin F. Cheatham.provenanceNote: 'impetuous' has one opened source (NPS series, an author's judgment). Other opened pages (ABT, Tennessee Encyclopedia) mention Bragg's accusation of drunkenness at Stones River ('appeared to be inebriated' / 'accused'), never proven and NOT used as evidence. The NPS series puts the broader piecemeal Round Forest attacks on Polk's corps and Bragg's orders, not Cheatham alone.

P. G. T. Beauregard.provenanceNote: Only one trait kept (fewer than 2). ABT's reason for the dusk halt is that he believed the army victorious, not fear; keep the game text to the conduct. 'methodical' dropped: see dropped.

evidence.claim: Before Shiloh Beauregard advised retiring to Corinth; at dusk on 6 April 1862 he halted the attacks, believing the army victorious, before Buell arrived overnight; on 29-30 May 1862 he evacuated Corinth without a serious battle, citing lack of water, disease and fear of encirclement.

The NPS Shiloh series and jfepperson.org's transcription of Special Orders No. 8 tie the parallel-corps order to Beauregard's plan/staff but do not state he wrote it, and jfepperson says only that it is signed by Jordan for Johnston and 'often criticized' for making command and control difficult. Williams's biography (book) was not opened. Unsupported, so dropped; also removes the Williams-vs-Daniel dispute that previously made him Disputed.

Gideon J. Pillow.provenanceNote: Only one trait kept (fewer than 2). The recall is better described as indecision: NPS says the escape route closed 'because of indecision and confusion among their commanders'; Civil War Monitor and ABT say Pillow ordered the troops back to the trenches; Monitor says he passed command to Buckner 'before fleeing by riverboat'. If the designers want a second trait, 'cautious' is supportable by those three pages, but it was not in the original list so it is not added here. The Stones River tree story is reported by ABT ('It was reported that...') and is not established.

evidence.claim: At daybreak 15 Feb 1862 at Fort Donelson Pillow led the breakout attack on McClernand's flank that briefly opened the Forge Road escape route; at Stones River NPS says his brigade 'was fighting well' on 2 Jan 1863.

His Donelson reversal was a pull-back (ABT: 'pull his men back into their trenches'; Monitor: 'ordered the troops to return to their trenches'), which reads as the opposite. The Breckinridge/tree anecdote concerns avoiding the fight, also not impetuous. Earlier 'Disputed' status (aggressive-but-vain vs cowardly) rested on unopened books.
